persp-horizon-one-point.summary: The horizon is your eye level, and every set of parallel lines that runs away from you aims at a vanishing point on it, unless the lines slope. You find horizons and vanishing points in photographs first, then build one-point rooms, tile floors and streets in which one face of every box faces you. It is the vocabulary every later perspective module assumes.

resources.notes: Studio Chalkboard's free perspective series. Work lessons 1 and 2 (introduction, one-point exteriors with horizon and vanishing points), then lessons 3 to 7 (interiors, a perfect square, circles, grids and tile floors, diminishing size). Redraw each construction yourself.
Read 4.2 and 4.3 (horizon, vanishing points, picture plane), then 4.4 and 4.5 on one-point, and try the matching practical assessments at the end of the chapter.

practice.description: Rule a one-point room grid on a page (a horizon, one vanishing point and evenly spaced floor lines), draw a bed, a table and a shelf on it, then redraw one of them freehand without the grid.

done_when.text: On an A4 printout of a photo, the horizon and vanishing point you place sit within about 1 cm of where two extended edges actually meet
Timed, you can set up a one-point room with a horizon, vanishing point and back wall in about two minutes

revisit.title: One-point room, cold
revisit.description: In two minutes set up a one-point room with the vanishing point somewhere you have not put it before. Add a tile floor by diagonals and two boxes standing on whole tiles.

@persp-two-point.p0.description: Draw one box five times, rotating it in steps from nearly square-on to nearly edge-on, keeping the same horizon. Mark both vanishing points each time and note how they shift, then turn a box the same way in the form viewer and compare.

done_when.text: Extended with a ruler, every set of parallel edges in a two-point drawing meets its vanishing point within about 1 cm on A4

revisit.title: Box and corner, cold
revisit.description: Draw a two-point box with both vanishing points off the page, then a building corner with one row of windows. Extend the edges with a ruler and check where they meet.

resources.notes: Drawabox Lesson 1 covers ellipses in planes; its cylinder challenge comes later. No research pass could read drawabox.com, so follow the lesson's own instructions.

A step-by-step method for an ellipse inside a square on a two-point box, with the minor axis through the centre and toward the vanishing point. A reply on the page notes it only works for a circle in a square (search-result evidence; not opened).

add_practice.title: Cylinder axis check in the form viewer
add_practice.description: In the form viewer, set a cylinder at an angle with the ellipse axes hidden. Draw it with the minor axis first, then switch on the ellipse axes and compare. Repeat at three heights relative to the horizon.

revisit.title: Cylinder at a new angle
revisit.description: Draw a box at a rotation you have not used, fit a cylinder in it with the minor axis drawn first, and add rings above and below eye level.

organic-forms-contours.summary: Organic forms are the soft volumes that plants, insects, animals and bodies are built from: sausages, eggs, teardrops and flattened balls. You draw them with smooth silhouettes, wrap contour lines around them so they read as 3D, overlap them, and join them with soft intersections. Drawabox teaches this in its Lesson 2, before plants, insects and animals.
learning_outcomes: Draw a sausage form (two equal balls joined by a tube) with an even width and a smooth silhouette
Wrap contour lines and ellipses around an organic form so they follow its surface and its turn toward or away from you
Overlap organic forms so one clearly sits in front of another
Join two organic forms with a soft intersection line that wraps around both

resources.notes: Drawabox Lesson 2 (Contour Lines, Texture and Construction) teaches organic forms with contour lines and form intersections; search results confirm the title and exercises, but no research pass could open the page. Do its organic-form and intersection sections.
Ctrl+Paint's assignment of laying form lines over photos of unusual bugs, drawing through the subject to find its volumes. A good second exercise once sausages feel easy.
Drawabox Lesson 4 opens its homework with two pages of organic forms with contours before any insect, which shows how this module feeds the animal modules (search-result evidence).

practice.title: Sausage page
practice.description: Draw 20 sausage forms (two equal balls joined by a tube) in different directions and lengths, some straight and some bent. Keep the width constant along each and the ends round; draw each side in one confident stroke.

practice.title: Contour lines on sausages
practice.description: On ten sausages, draw the central flow line, then three to five contour curves that wrap around the form and an ellipse at each end. Make the curves more open where the form turns away from you and flatter where it faces you.

practice.title: Overlap pile
practice.description: Pile up five to eight eggs, teardrops and sausages so that they overlap. Where one passes in front, its silhouette runs unbroken and cuts the one behind. Add contour lines to each.

practice.title: Soft joins
practice.description: Draw pairs of organic forms meeting: an egg pushed into a ball, a sausage growing out of a bean, two teardrops fused at the tips. Draw the intersection line wrapping around both forms, and soften it where they blend.

practice.title: Fruit and vegetables as organic forms
practice.description: Draw a pepper, a banana and a pear from life as organic forms with contour lines before you commit to their outlines.

done_when.text: On a page of 20 sausage forms, most keep a constant width with round ends and no pinched middles
Contour lines change along each form: flatter where the surface faces you, more curved where it turns away
In an overlap pile, every junction reads the right way when you check them one by one
Soft intersection lines wrap around both forms instead of sitting on one of them like a sticker

common_mistakes: Contour lines that run past the silhouette or stop short of it, so they float on the surface
Drawing every contour curve at the same degree, which flattens the form
Pinched or swollen sausages from drawing the two sides as unrelated lines
Too many contour lines; three to five that describe the turn do more than twenty
Going over the silhouette again and again to fix it instead of drawing the next form

revisit.title: Three forms, wrapped
revisit.description: Draw three new organic forms (a bent sausage, a teardrop, an egg) overlapping each other, add contour lines, and join two of them with a soft intersection.

resources.notes: Drawabox Lesson 6 applies construction to everyday objects from your own home. Drawabox places it after its plant and animal lessons; use it here if you prefer objects first (search-result evidence; not opened).
Optional, only if you have done the 3D blockout module: Blender's Boolean modifier unions or subtracts one solid from another, which shows additive and subtractive construction in 3D.

@persp-construct-primitives.p2.description: Start from a box or cylinder and carve it: a notch, a hole, a bevel, a slot. Draw six variations. Then set the starting form in the form viewer, orbit to a second view and redraw one carved version from there. Optional, if you have done the 3D blockout module: model two in Blender with a difference Boolean and compare.

done_when.text: Timed, you can break an everyday object into six or fewer primitives within five minutes

revisit.title: Object as primitives, cold
revisit.description: Pick a household object you have not built before. In five minutes list its primitives and draw it transparently, then redraw it from a second angle using only your construction.

persp-depth-cues.summary: Before any vanishing point appears, a drawing already suggests depth through overlap, relative size, placement on the page, distant values and detail fading, and shapes that read as flat or round. You learn to name these cues in other people's pictures and to use them on purpose with one overlap ladder and one atmospheric ladder, and to choose a horizon height deliberately.

revisit.title: Three planes, no lines
revisit.description: Draw a new landscape or street thumbnail in three planes using only overlap, size and value fade, with no perspective lines. Then name the cue doing most of the work.

nat-everyday-objects.summary: Ordinary objects are built from cylinders, boxes and spheres with handles, hinges and openings added. You practise ellipses for bottles and cups, boxes for furniture, simple mechanisms for tools, and soft shapes for bags and cushions. Soft goods follow the same fold logic as the drapery module.

resources.notes: Drawabox Lesson 6 asks for objects from your own home built with construction, which is better practice than copying photos. Do it once boxes and ellipses feel steady (search-result evidence; not opened).

revisit.title: Mug and chair, cold
revisit.description: Draw a mug with a handle and a chair from objects in the room that you have not drawn before, each built from primitives first, about four minutes each.

invent-objects-2.summary: Take invention past single objects: rotate an invented object to any view, fuse two remembered objects into one, and redesign an object for a new user or job while keeping it buildable. Construction from primitives carries the drawing, and every invention ends with a check against reference or the form viewer. Studying master prints for their structure, not their surface, feeds the library you invent from.
learning_outcomes: Rotate an invented object through four views that agree with each other
Redesign an everyday object for a stated user or purpose while keeping its parts buildable
Check an invention against reference or a 3D view and name what you guessed wrong

resources.notes: Proko's perspective course: use the free lessons, especially the assignment on perspective for drawing anything and the free critique 'Collecting Masters', which is about building a library of structures to invent from.
Marshall Vandruff and Stan Prokopenko on learning perspective so you can use it without reference (free episode, 53:47).

practice.title: Four-view turnaround of an invented object
practice.description: Invent an object from primitives, then draw it from the front, three-quarter, side and from above. Carry its main proportions between views with light horizontal guide lines.

practice.title: Redesign for a user
practice.description: Pick an everyday object (a torch, a chair, a kettle) and redesign it three ways: for a child, for a deep-sea diver, for a robot. Keep the base primitives visible and change the proportions, handles and attachments.

practice.title: Scaffold in the form viewer
practice.description: Block out an invented scene in the form viewer with boxes and cylinders and choose a camera. Then draw the scene from a different viewpoint without looking, and check afterwards.

practice.title: Invent, then check against reference
practice.description: Draw from imagination an object you have not studied (a sewing machine, a lantern, a microscope). Then find two photos, mark what you guessed wrong in a second colour, and redraw it from the same view.

done_when.text: Extended with a ruler, the box edges of an invented object converge consistently in each of its four views, within about 1 cm on A4
Your four views of one invented object agree on proportions when you lay a ruler across matching parts
A fused object shows where its two sources join, with an intersection line that wraps around both forms
You can tell the difference between recalling a structure and merely copying a memorised outline
After checking an invention against two photos you can name what you guessed wrong, and the redrawn version fixes it

common_mistakes: Waiting until construction feels steady before drawing from imagination; draw from imagination every week, then check against reference
Fusing objects by gluing outlines side by side instead of joining the forms
Letting proportions drift between views when rotating an invented object

revisit.title: Rotate one invention
revisit.description: Take an object you invented earlier. In seven minutes draw it from a view you have not drawn, then lay a ruler across matching parts to compare proportions with the earlier drawing.

done_when.text: On a flat floor, the horizon cuts every same-height figure at the same body point when checked with a ruler

revisit.title: Fence and figures
revisit.description: Draw a receding fence of seven posts placed by diagonals, and three people at different distances on the same ground. Check with a ruler that the horizon cuts each person at the same body height.

@persp-three-point.p4.description: Set up a three-point grid on a large page, with the third vanishing point off the page edge if it has to be, draw two simple buildings on it, then draw a third building without the grid.

done_when.text: In a bird's-eye block drawn without construction, the verticals of four buildings meet within 1 cm of one third point when extended with a ruler

revisit.title: Towers from below
revisit.description: Draw a box tilted upward and two towers sharing three vanishing points, then extend every vertical with a ruler to the third point.

@persp-parallel-projection.p2.description: Build the same object in the form viewer from boxes and cylinders, set the longest focal length so lines barely converge, and view it straight from the front, top and side; or use SketchUp Free's standard views. Compare with your drawings.

revisit.title: Three views, one object
revisit.description: Pick a small object you have not drawn. Draw its front, top and side views so they agree, then an isometric drawing built from them.

@persp-curvilinear.p0.description: Draw a circle and mark four points on its rim at the compass points plus one at its centre. Draw curved lines from each rim point through the circle to build a grid, then check that each family of curves meets at its own rim point and that the two lines through the centre stay straight.

@persp-curvilinear.p3.description: Build a curvilinear grid by hand as in the first exercise, or use Krita's curvilinear assistant if you draw digitally, and draw a street scene on it. Then redraw it by hand without the grid.

revisit.title: Fisheye cube
revisit.description: Draw a five-point grid by hand without a template, then a cube at its centre and another near the rim, and check which edges stay straight.

simple-3d-blockout.summary: A 3D blockout is a quick scene of boxes, cylinders and spheres in free 3D software, used as drawing reference: you choose the camera and the light, then draw from the screen or check a drawing against it. This module covers the minimum in Blender (navigate, add primitives, one light, a camera, a screenshot) and in a free posable figure tool. No other module requires it; every exercise also works with the app's own form, light and mannequin tools.
learning_outcomes: Navigate a 3D view: orbit, pan, zoom, and switch between perspective and orthographic
Add, move, scale and rotate boxes, cylinders and spheres to block out an object or a simple scene
Place one light and a camera, then save a screenshot to draw from
Pose a figure in a free posable figure tool and frame it from a chosen camera height

resources.notes: Blender is free and open source. You need only a fraction of it: the viewport, adding primitives, moving and scaling them, one light and one camera.
Blender's manual page on light objects. Read the point and sun light parts; ignore the rest for now.
A posable figure app with a free tier. Pose a figure, then move the camera low and high to see how the pose changes.
Optional: the Boolean modifier carves one solid out of another, which helps when you draw subtractive construction.

practice.title: First blockout
practice.description: In Blender, add a floor plane and three primitives: a box, a cylinder and a sphere. Move and scale them into a simple still life, then orbit around it and find three views worth drawing. The app's form viewer does the same with fewer controls.

practice.title: One light, three positions
practice.description: Add one sun or point light and move it to three positions: high side, low side and behind. Take a screenshot of each and draw one in three tones. The light tool in Delineare shows the same kind of set-up in greys.

practice.title: Predict the camera
practice.description: Add a camera. Before looking through it, sketch what you expect the scene to look like from there, then look, take a screenshot and compare. Repeat from a low and a high camera.

practice.title: Pose and frame a figure
practice.description: In a free posable figure tool or the app's mannequin, pose a figure reaching for something on a shelf. Frame it from a low camera and a high camera and draw both as simple boxes and cylinders.

practice.title: Optional: carve with a Boolean
practice.description: In Blender, cut a notch and a hole out of a box with a difference Boolean, orbit to two views and draw them. Compare with a version you drew first from imagination.

done_when.text: You can orbit, pan and zoom a 3D view and switch it between perspective and orthographic without looking up the controls
You have built one blockout of at least three primitives with one light and saved screenshots from two camera angles
Overlaid at 50 percent, a drawing made from your blockout screenshot has its box edges within about 1 cm of the screenshot's on A4
You can pose a figure in a posable figure tool and frame it from a low and a high camera

common_mistakes: Spending the session learning software features instead of drawing
Tracing the screenshot's outline instead of constructing the forms you see
Leaving a very wide camera lens on by accident, which stretches forms near the edges
Lighting with many lights, so the forms lose a clear light side and shadow side

revisit.title: Predict a new view
revisit.description: Pick a camera angle you have not used on your blockout or in the form viewer. Draw what you predict the forms will look like, then show the view and overlay your drawing on a screenshot.
